findings.title: JWS algorithm/key confusion: asymmetric public key accepted as HMAC secret
findings.explanation: When a token header specifies an HMAC algorithm (HS256/384/512), jws.verify builds an HMACKey out of whatever verification key the application supplied. To stop an attacker from exploiting the classic alg-confusion attack (signing an HS256 token with the victim's *public* key as the shared secret), HMACKey.__init__ blocklists key material that looks like a public key. The blocklist only rejects PEM-wrapped keys ('-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----', '-----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY-----', '-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----') and OpenSSH RSA ('ssh-rsa'). It does NOT reject OpenSSH-format ECDSA public keys ('ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521'), Ed25519 ('ssh-ed25519'), or DSS ('ssh-dss') public keys. An application that verifies with an ECDSA/Ed25519 public key stored in OpenSSH authorized_keys format while allowing HS256 in its algorithm list lets an attacker — who knows the (public) key — forge arbitrary tokens: they compute HMAC-SHA256(public_key_bytes, header.payload) and the signature verifies. This is an authentication bypass (CVE-2024-33663).

findings.title: JWS algorithm/key confusion: asymmetric public key accepted as HMAC secret (cryptography backend)
findings.explanation: Same algorithm/key-confusion flaw as in the native backend, in the preferred (default) cryptography backend. CryptographyHMACKey.__init__ guards against an asymmetric public key being used as an HMAC secret with a blocklist that only catches PEM public keys/certificates and 'ssh-rsa'. OpenSSH-format ECDSA ('ecdsa-sha2-*'), Ed25519 ('ssh-ed25519'), and DSS public keys pass the check and are accepted as the raw HMAC secret. An application verifying JWS/JWT with such a public key while permitting an HMAC algorithm can be tricked into accepting attacker-forged HS256 tokens, because the attacker can compute the HMAC using the publicly known key bytes. This is an authentication/signature-verification bypass (CVE-2024-33663).

findings.title: JWE decompression bomb: unbounded zlib.decompress on attacker-controlled ciphertext
findings.explanation: jwe.decrypt accepts a compact JWE string from an untrusted source. When the (attacker-chosen) protected header contains "zip":"DEF", the decrypted plaintext is passed to _decompress, which calls zlib.decompress with no limit on output size. A small, highly compressible payload (a 'zip bomb') can be crafted to inflate to gigabytes, exhausting memory and causing a denial of service. Because the attacker fully controls both the compression flag and the ciphertext, and only needs to be able to produce a valid JWE for a key the recipient uses (e.g. 'dir' with a shared symmetric key, or any public-key alg), the amplification happens before any application-level size check. This is CVE-2024-33664.
